name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
title: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
answer: Institutional knowledge graphs represent the entities an organization cares about, such as people, projects, publications, datasets, instruments, and administrative units, and the relationships among them. They are built to answer questions that span silos, for example which datasets support a given publication or which researchers collaborate on a grant. In a research data and repositories context, the graph often includes vocabularies, licenses, and provenance records so that a resource can be traced from creation to reuse. A repository with 135 research papers and 12,993 extracted claims, like this site, illustrates how quickly a graph can grow once claims and citations become primary nodes. The scope is not the whole web but the institution's own holdings and the external identifiers that anchor them.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs represent the entities an organization cares about, such as people, projects, publications, datasets, instruments, and administrative units, and the relationships among them. They are built to answer questions that span silos, for example which datasets support a given publication or which researchers collaborate on a grant. In a research data and repositories context, the graph often includes vocabularies, licenses, and provenance records so that a resource can be traced from creation to reuse. A repository with 135 research papers and 12,993 extracted claims, like this site, illustrates how quickly a graph can grow once claims and citations become primary nodes. The scope is not the whole web but the institution's own holdings and the external identifiers that anchor them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The graph runs on a storage layer that supports either RDF triples or property graphs, with query languages such as SPARQL or Cypher. It depends on persistent identifiers like DOIs, ORCID iDs, and ROR IDs to keep entities stable across systems. Common components include an ontology or schema, an ingestion pipeline, a triple store or graph database, and APIs that let repository platforms and discovery interfaces read the graph. Many institutions also keep a search index alongside the graph because graph queries alone are not ideal for search over free text. The infrastructure is usually integrated with existing repository software, identity management, and data catalogues rather than replacing them.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with identifying authoritative sources, such as a research information system, a repository, a grant management system, and a vocabulary service. Teams then map those sources to a shared ontology, extract entities and relationships, and resolve duplicates so that the same person or dataset is not represented twice. Extraction can be manual, rules based, or assisted by machine learning, but every asserted relationship should carry a provenance link back to its source record. A graph with 12,993 claims from 135 papers, as on this site, shows why automated extraction needs review and why provenance at the claim level matters. The graph is then loaded, queried, and refined in cycles as new publications, datasets, and corrections arrive.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk management for an institutional knowledge graph starts with knowing the license and access conditions of every source. Some nodes and edges may be public, some restricted to the institution, and some subject to privacy rules, so the graph needs access control at the query level, not just at the interface. Provenance is recorded as part of the graph so that a user can see who asserted a relationship, when, and from which source. Risks include identifying individuals from combined data, stale or incorrect links, and relying too much on a graph that mixes authoritative and experimental sources. Institutions typically define stewardship roles, change logs, and review processes to keep the graph trustworthy.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward federation, where institutional graphs answer queries across multiple organizations without centralizing all data. FAIR principles and persistent identifiers are pushing graphs to be more interoperable, and repository systems are beginning to expose graph endpoints as a standard feature. Machine learning is being used to suggest new links and to extract entities from text, but human review remains part of the workflow for assertions with high impact. Expect more integration between knowledge graphs and the tools researchers already use, such as discovery portals, data catalogues, and reporting dashboards. The aim over time is a graph that is useful for everyday tasks, not a separate destination that only specialists visit.
